failure_summary.description: Clue said 'current king'. The agent chose today's holder (Abdullah II) instead of the person the passages tie to the distinctive details (Harrow & Sandhurst, Infoplease 'Hussein I ... educated at Harrow and Sandhurst'). Archive clues are frozen in time, and the skill's 'outdated descriptor' guidance covers only superlatives.

The agent answered 'Denver Mint' where the key was 'Denver'. The 'keep the head noun' exception for 'this empire/gland/purchase' was over-applied to 'this mint', where the bare place name is a complete answer.

The correct person, King Hussein, is known only by a given name plus title, and the key keeps the title ('King Hussein'). The skill's blanket rule to drop 'king' could produce a bare, ambiguous 'Hussein'.

patch.reasoning: Both failures come from rules that were applied wrongly or were incomplete. (1) Time-relative words in archive-style clues ('current', 'present', 'now') are frozen at the clue's airing date. The agent should anchor on the distinctive biographical details and the passage that matches them, not on who holds the office today. (2) For 'this mint / river / airport / university' clues, the bare proper name is the expected answer, so the head-noun exception needs a narrowing clarification. (3) Rulers known only by a given name need the title kept, so the 'drop the role word' rule needs a carve-out for them.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content: - Time-relative words in the clue ('current', 'present', 'now', 'today', 'new', 'latest') are frozen at the date the clue was written. Do NOT answer with today's holder of the office. Anchor on the distinctive biographical or factual details (schools, birthplace, deeds) and choose the person the passages tie to them, even if that person is no longer 'current'. Example: 'This current king of Jordan ... educated at Harrow & Sandhurst' -> the passage 'Hussein I, king of Jordan; educated in England at Harrow and Sandhurst' wins over the present-day king. A near-verbatim passage match on the clue's details beats the 'current' wording.

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - Places and institutions: when the clue says 'this mint / port / river / lake / mountain / airport / college / university / bank / prison / bridge / island / county', the answer key almost always uses the bare proper name. 'whose mark is a "D"' + 'this mint' -> 'Denver' (not 'Denver Mint'); 'this river' -> 'Nile'; 'this university' -> 'Yale'. Strike the type word the clue already gives (mint, river, college) even if the passages write 'Denver Mint'. Keep a head noun only when the bare word names a different thing or is not a complete name ('Roman Empire', 'Gadsden Purchase', 'pituitary gland').

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Rulers known by only a given name: when the answer is a monarch, pope or similar whom the passages call by a single given name (no surname) and the clue says 'this king/queen/pope', keep the title with the name ('King Hussein', 'Queen Victoria'), because the bare given name is ambiguous across dynasties. If a full name or surname exists ('Winston Churchill'), give it without the title.
